title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
content: Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands. The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year. It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have fallen in recent days over concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment. Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period. The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row. Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology. Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI. Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply. In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%. Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. Trading on South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq was temporarily halted after falling by more than 8%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by over 5%. The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending. Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino". There also been concerns over the safety of AI models. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety. The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn. Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down . The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday. The developers, Evolution Power Limited, say the two sites could attract £25bn of investment. Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US. Palantir drops its case after City Hall says blocking the £50m Met deal was not about its values. Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI. Newbury Street Practice, in Wantage, began using the AI Andi triage system in July. title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
content: Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years. The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything". She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise . Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers for September that were released on Wednesday. The price rise was more than economists and Wall Street analysts had forecast. High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans. Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family. "I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark." Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money. And it is still not enough to support her family. Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home. "I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said. The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult. And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline. "I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said. Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control." He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up. The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, the index was -40. In May, it reached -45, the lowest since 2022. A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis. This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that. When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef." As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said. Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken. "[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said. Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month. "I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically." For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming. She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies. Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice. The family has even decided to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much. "It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot." Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived. Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US. Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated. The school has faced an uproar over how it handled assault allegations brought by a woman known as Jane Doe. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died on Monday after police say he was ejected from a ride at an amusement park. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
content: Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds. The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said. Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £45,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships. It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate. Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment. Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA. The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds. Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March. The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added. The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%. The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing . A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers". Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead. Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics. "When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added. Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics. "Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines." Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response. "The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said. The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways. Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers. However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false. Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines. Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said. Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that didn't appear. The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide. The leadership team is attempting a buyout, but a union has warned the retailer could fall into administration instead. The influential economics body has upgraded its UK growth forecast for this year, but risks remain. TFG London has apologised to customers for disruption after it identified a "cybersecurity incident" on Sunday. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
content: On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China". Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes. Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry. In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting. The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business. Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed. Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it." Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months. So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang. On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes. Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it. Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour. He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive." And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises. Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report at the start of this year. Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so. The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories. Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries. From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong. Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance. Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September. Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents. Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more. This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents. This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China. "We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg. The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total. That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys. "It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says. If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each. While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50. Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey. China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces. Can Nepal bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in the Himalayas? The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs. As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support. A new industry being dubbed the “loneliness economy” has emerged in China, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
content: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount . Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. "Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. You can also get in touch by following this link Apurv Patel is one of several people who say they were promised job opportunities that didn't appear. The Competition and Markets Authority has fined Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym £6m in total. The leadership team is attempting a buyout, but a union has warned the retailer could fall into administration instead. title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
content: Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years. Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10. Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City. The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly". The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives". The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers". "We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do." The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year. None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC. It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports. Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport. "Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports. She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution". The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports. Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households. The path between Thornhill and Penpont is meant to be used by cyclists, walkers and wheelchair users. Council appeals for interested parties to apply for £100,000 funding after Towcester bus link ends. Hugh Spence says taking part in a test bus journey feels like he has been "listened to". The hotel on what was Wakefield Westgate rail station will "meet growing demand", the council says. Thomas Woldbye tells the Today progamme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after comments made by the prime minister. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
content: US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US. Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%. Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy. The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change. There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise. If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example. Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices. Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel. Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100. Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices. Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months. In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year. Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%. Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027. The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month. The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December. Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world. While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year. While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years. During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up. Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel. Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%. It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace. A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates. Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions. Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand. With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves. US inflation continues to rise, and this month the jump was above forecasts. Here's how some are surviving. With the ongoing war in the Middle East increasing prices, one deputy is ask for duty to be frozen. On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised UK plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing. title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
content: Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures. But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about." The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn . The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing. Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects. Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them. But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test. Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand." She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks. "On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken." Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure. Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog". "While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added. A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017". "But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added. Copyright 2026 BBC. title: Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
content: "Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand. The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities. In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US. On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised the UK's plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting. "The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier. Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out". The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level. It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits. This matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments. While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock. This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions. It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households. Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
